summary:
MARSCOPE is an interactive, browser-based planetary exploration dashboard and human survival decision-support platform designed for the Red Planet. 

Surviving and operating on Mars requires synthesizing complex, disparate datasets across extreme diurnal temperature swings (-125°C to 20°C), unshielded radiation, and sparse water-ice reserves. To address this challenge, MARSCOPE integrates authentic orbital telemetry and Web Map Tile Service (WMTS) layers directly from NASA Mars Trek, MGS MOLA elevation topography, and USGS planetary geologic maps (SIM 3292) into a unified, zero-install mission console.

The platform features an algorithmic habitability engine that calculates coordinate-specific landing safety, thermal gradients, solar insolation, and proximity to Odyssey GRS and MRO SHARAD water-ice deposits. Complementing the GIS engine, MARSCOPE provides an interactive Base Site Planner, historical rover traverse tracking, great-circle geodesic route planning, and an astronaut survival equipment logistics calculator.

MARSCOPE bridges the gap between raw scientific archives and practical mission architecture, empowering students, researchers, and future explorers to evaluate viable pathways toward a sustainable human presence on Mars.
details:
1. What does MARSCOPE do and how does it work?

MARSCOPE is an interactive, browser-based planetary exploration console and human survival decision-support system for Mars. Built with standard web technologies (vanilla ES modules and Leaflet GIS), it streams high-resolution orbital telemetry directly from NASA Mars Trek Web Map Tile Services (WMTS).

Key architectural components include:

• Planetary Multi-Layer GIS: Synchronizes MOLA shaded elevation relief, Viking true-color mosaics (MDIM 2.1), and USGS planetary chronostratigraphic geologic maps (SIM 3292) across an equirectangular projection.

• Survival Suitability Engine: A multi-criteria mathematical model that evaluates coordinates in real time based on latitude, thermal gradients, solar insolation, terrain slope safety (<15° threshold), and proximity to verified Odyssey GRS and MRO SHARAD subsurface water-ice deposits.

• Mission Explorer & Traverses: An interactive database of historic landers, orbiters, and active rover traverses (Perseverance, Curiosity, Opportunity) with scientific stop telemetry.

• Route & Logistics Tooling: Features great-circle geodesic surface distance calculation between waypoints, an Astronaut Emergency Mode with simulated environmental stress protocols, and an interactive payload mass calculator ("Pack Your Mars Kit").

2. What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

• Democratizing Planetary Science: Raw scientific archives (PDS, MOLA, SHARAD) are often locked in specialized GIS formats. MARSCOPE transforms this data into an intuitive, zero-install educational tool for students, educators, and space enthusiasts.

• Mission Architecture Decision-Support: Demonstrates how multi-criteria spatial analysis aids preliminary human landing site evaluation (e.g., Arcadia Planitia vs. Jezero Crater), illustrating the critical trade-offs between solar power availability and water-ice proximity for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU).

• Instant Global Accessibility: 100% client-side architecture requiring no runtime setup, compiler, or account sign-in, running smoothly across desktop, tablet, and mobile browsers.

3. How is the project creative and novel?

Rather than functioning as a passive map or static infographic, MARSCOPE couples spatial planetary cartography with interactive survival engineering simulations. Users do not merely view coordinates—they drop pins to simulate localized survivability scores (0–100), analyze radiation and diurnal thermal stress, plan multi-leg rover expeditions, and configure spacecraft payload budgets under realistic mass constraints.

4. What environmental factors did our team consider?

Our habitability algorithms and simulation modules account for:

• Severe Diurnal Thermal Swings: Extreme drops down to -125°C at high latitudes and nightfall.

• Atmospheric & Radiation Hazards: Surface pressure at ~0.6% of Earth’s with zero ozone layer, exposing surface operations to unshielded solar UV and cosmic ray doses (~200 μGy/day).

• In-Situ Water Ice Accessibility: Prioritizing shallow permafrost and glacial reserves for drinking water, oxygen generation (MOXIE-class systems), and rocket propellant synthesis.

• Surface Morphology & Slope Hazards: Terrain roughness, crater rim gradients, and dune fields that pose rover mobility or lander touchdown hazards.

5. Tools, Coding Languages & Data Architecture

• Frontend Architecture: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3 (responsive mission-control dark design system), ES6+ JavaScript modules.

• Mapping & GIS Engine: Leaflet.js with custom EPSG:4326 Mars projection handlers and WMTS raster tile streaming.

• Mathematical Modeling: Spherical trigonometry (Haversine formula calibrated to Mars radius 3,389.5 km), solar zenith angle formulas, and weighted multi-factor decision matrices.

• Data Pipeline: Python scripts for caching and parsing NASA MMGIS rover traverse GeoJSON data.

• Deployment: Continuous deployment via Vercel / Netlify.
dataRefs: NASA Mars Trek Web Map Tile Services (WMTS)
NASA MGS MOLA — Used in the Base Site Planner & Terrain Engine to calculate surface elevation, slope roughness, and landing hazards
NASA 2001 Mars Odyssey GRS — Used in the Survival Model to map near-surface hydrogen & permafrost for ISRU drinking water potential
NASA MRO SHARAD Radar — Used in the Resource Overlay to pinpoint buried glacial ice sheets in mid-latitude regions like Arcadia Planitia
NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) — Used in the Mission Explorer & Rover Tracker for authentic landing coordinates and sol-by-sol traverse paths
projectRefs: USGS Planetary Geologic Map (SIM 3292) — Used in the Geologic Layer to display Noachian, Hesperian, and Amazonian bedrock stratigraphy
USGS Astrogeology Viking Mosaic (MDIM 2.1) — Used for the global true-color surface imagery layer
IAU / USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature — Used in the Search Bar and Map Labels for official crater, mountain, and canyon coordinates
